subtype: Living for the moment with costs [Actor]
passage:
Sumit, 11:42 pm: I did it. Walked out of the call centre tonight. Told the shift lead I'm done.
Yash: Wait, what? You said last week you'd stick it out till the course fees were sorted.
Sumit: He shouted at me in front of the whole floor for a customer's mistake. I just stood up and left.
Sumit: Also booked the Goa trip with Rohan's gang on the way home. Felt amazing for about an hour.
Yash: And now?
Sumit: Now I'm staring at my account and my chest feels tight. Rent is due on the fifth.
Yash: Okay. Breathe, bhai. Nothing more gets decided tonight, deal? Can you check tomorrow if the trip booking can be cancelled?
Sumit: Yeah. And maybe I call the manager, not the shift lead, and ask if the resignation actually went through.
Yash: Good. Next time you're that angry, text me before you do anything big. I'll just say "sleep on it".
Sumit: Sleep on it. Got it. Thanks, bro 🙏

qa.q: What did Sumit book on the way home?
qa.a: He booked the Goa trip with Rohan's gang on the way home.

qa.q: How was Sumit feeling after the first hour had passed?
qa.a: He was anxious and regretful; he says his chest feels tight as he stares at his account with rent due on the fifth.

qa.q: What small habit could stop Sumit making another big decision in a rage?
qa.a: Building in a delay, like texting Yash and sleeping on it before quitting or spending, gives the anger time to cool so he can choose calmly.

qa.q: How does Yash seem to see Sumit's night?
qa.a: Yash is worried but steady; he doesn't scold Sumit and instead helps him pause and plan small fixes for the next day.

grounding: Sumit quits his job in anger and spends on a trip in the rush of the moment, then a friend helps him build a delay habit.

passage:
The waiting room at the community counselling centre smelled of tea and floor polish. Sabina held the appointment slip so tightly it creased.
"Third time this year," she said quietly. "First the second-hand motorbike, then he paid a deposit on a flat without asking. Yesterday he signed up for a franchise course."
Francis rubbed his neck. "Each one felt like a door closing if I didn't jump."
"I know. But I lie awake doing sums, Francis."
When the counsellor called them in, Sabina did not list his failures. She said, "I want us to agree that anything above a set amount waits two days and we talk first."
Francis nodded slowly. "And if I push, you say 'two days', not 'you always'."
The counsellor wrote both lines down and asked them to try it for a month, then come back and see how it went.

qa.q: Where were Sabina and Francis waiting?
qa.a: They were in the waiting room at the community counselling centre.

qa.q: What does Sabina's grip on the appointment slip suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is anxious and tense; she admits she lies awake doing sums after his repeated sudden choices.

qa.q: Which part of Sabina's approach helps most, and why?
qa.a: She proposes a calm agreement about big decisions instead of listing his failures, so Francis can agree without feeling attacked.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis when a chance appears?
qa.a: He feels a door is closing if he doesn't jump, so waiting feels like loss to him, which is why a clear rule and a kinder reminder help him.

grounding: Sabina, affected by Francis's repeated rash choices about shared money, makes a calm agreement with him and they seek professional guidance.

passage:
Monday. Pankaj pressed his nose to the car window. "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" When Mama said the ice cream shop was after the bridge, he kicked the seat and cried.
Wednesday. Before leaving for Nani's, Mama gave him a paper strip with five stickers. "Each time we pass a petrol pump, peel one off." Pankaj counted pumps and asked only twice.
Saturday. Damini, his cousin, whined in the queue for the merry-go-round. Pankaj took her hand. "Let's sing the elephant song. When it ends, we'll be closer." They sang it three times, and then it was their turn.

qa.q: What did Mama give Pankaj on Wednesday?
qa.a: She gave him a paper strip with five stickers to peel off at each petrol pump.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj kick the seat and cry on Monday?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient; the ice cream shop still felt far away and he could not bear the wait.

qa.q: What could a parent borrow from Mama's idea for a long wait?
qa.a: They could make the wait something a child can see and count, like stickers, a song or a small game.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Pankaj starts singing with her in the queue?
qa.a: She probably feels comforted and less bored, because the song gives the wait a clear end she can hear.

grounding: Pankaj's crying over a delayed treat eases as adults make waiting concrete with stickers and songs, which he later shares with his cousin.

passage:
Thomas had wanted the remote-control jeep in the window of the toy shop near Malad station since Diwali. It cost more than three months of his pocket money.
Every Sunday, when Papa handed him his coins, Thomas stood at the ice-cream cart for a long moment, then walked on. He dropped the money into an old tea tin and wrote the new total on a strip of tape.
In February his friend Sumit bought a spinning top the day he got money and lost it in a week. Thomas felt a small sting of envy, then looked at the tape.
In April he carried the tin to the shop himself. The shopkeeper counted it twice. Thomas walked home holding the box against his chest, grinning, and told Papa, "I waited, and it was worth it."

qa.q: Where did Thomas keep his saved coins?
qa.a: He dropped them into an old tea tin and wrote the total on a strip of tape.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling as he walked home in April?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy; he was grinning and holding the box to his chest because his waiting had paid off.

qa.q: What helped Thomas keep going through the months?
qa.a: Writing the new total on the tape each week let him see his progress, which made walking past the ice-cream cart easier.

qa.q: How might Papa see Thomas's months of saving?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel proud that Thomas learned for himself that waiting can bring something bigger.

grounding: Thomas saves his pocket money for a toy, learns that waiting brings more, and enjoys the pride of having managed it.

passage:
Week one, Tuesday. Aparna finished her first practice run around the colony gate gasping and slow. At home she checked the running app screen, groaned and told her sister Preeti, "Pointless. Everyone in the club runs twice as far."
Week three, Thursday. She had skipped two sessions. Preeti found her scrolling through other runners' times. "Stop comparing. Open your own notebook. What did you do on day one?" Aparna flipped back. One round, stopping twice.
Week seven, Sunday. Aparna ran three rounds without stopping. She did not check anyone else's times. She wrote the date, drew a small star, and texted Preeti a photo of the page: "Day one me would not believe this." Preeti replied with a thumbs-up and "Told you, slow is still moving."

qa.q: How many rounds did Aparna run without stopping in week seven?
qa.a: She ran three rounds without stopping.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel after her first practice run?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and impatient; she called it pointless because others in the club ran twice as far.

qa.q: What changed Aparna's approach between week three and week seven?
qa.a: She stopped comparing herself to others and tracked her own small steps in her notebook, which made slow progress visible.

qa.q: How does Preeti see her sister's struggle?
qa.a: Preeti seems patient and caring; she nudges Aparna to look back at her own day one instead of giving up.

grounding: Aparna nearly gives up on running when progress is slow, then builds patience by comparing herself only to her earlier self.

passage:
The power had gone out in the housing office, and the queue for the property transfer snaked into the corridor. Tenzin had brought his grandmother-in-law, Ganga Amma, whose name had to be on the forms.
She read every line aloud, slowly, and asked the clerk the same question twice. A man behind them sighed loudly.
Tenzin felt the heat rise in his own neck, too. He could have taken the pen and signed where the clerk pointed. Instead he crouched beside her chair. "Take your time, Amma. We have the whole afternoon."
The clerk, sweating in the dark room, softened and explained again. Ganga Amma signed, smiled, and patted Tenzin's hand.
It took three hours. On the bus home Tenzin checked the next step, booked the follow-up date on his phone, and let her doze on his shoulder.

qa.q: Why was the room at the housing office dark?
qa.a: The power had gone out in the housing office.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when the man behind them sighed?
qa.a: He felt irritated and hot too, but he chose to stay calm and crouch beside Ganga Amma rather than rush her.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's patience do well in this scene?
qa.a: It lets Ganga Amma understand what she signs and even softens the clerk, while Tenzin still books the next step, so the process keeps moving.

qa.q: How might Ganga Amma see the afternoon?
qa.a: She likely felt respected and safe, since nobody took the pen from her and she could ask her questions.

grounding: Tenzin stays calm with a slow elder and a long process in a hot, powerless office, choosing pace with purpose rather than passivity.

subtype: Big feelings in a small body [Actor]
passage:
Clara, two, saw the ducks at the pond in Leeds and shrieked with joy, flapping her arms.
When her dad said it was time to go, she dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing. Wei did not shout. He crouched beside her. "You loved those ducks. It's hard to leave."
He waited, one hand near her back. Slowly her kicks stopped. She crawled onto his knee and waved. "Bye, ducks."

qa.q: What did Clara do when it was time to go?
qa.a: She dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing.

qa.q: How was Clara feeling when she lay on the path?
qa.a: She was angry and upset about leaving the ducks, and too small to calm down on her own.

qa.q: What helped Clara settle, and why might it work?
qa.a: Wei stayed close and calm, named her feeling and waited, so she could borrow his calm until her body slowed.

qa.q: How might Wei feel while Clara kicks and wails on the path?
qa.a: He may feel tired or tense, but he chooses to stay calm and close so she can learn to settle.

grounding: Toddler Clara shows intense joy and rage over small things and settles through her dad's calm presence.

passage:
Jahnavi loved her new puppy so much she made him a birthday card on his first week home. So when Rohit laughed at the card in class, saying only babies make cards for dogs, she ran out of the room.
It was the last day before the exams, the teacher was busy with revision, and the corridor was noisy with the cleaners. Jahnavi cried loudly by the water cooler.
Jaya Ma'am, the class teacher, found her there between periods. She had only five minutes. "You're hurt and embarrassed, right?" Jahnavi nodded, sobbing. "Let's cool the fire first. Breathe in like smelling a flower, out like blowing a candle." They did it four times.
"Your big love for that puppy is a good thing," Jaya Ma'am said. "We'll talk to Rohit after the bell." Jahnavi wiped her face and walked back in.

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi cry after running out of class?
qa.a: She cried loudly by the water cooler in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Rohit's joke hit Jahnavi so hard?
qa.a: She loved her puppy fiercely, so the teasing made her feel deeply hurt and embarrassed, not just a little annoyed.

qa.q: What did Jaya Ma'am do that could help Jahnavi next time?
qa.a: She named the feelings and taught a quick breathing way to cool down, which Jahnavi can use herself even when adults are busy.

qa.q: If you were Rohit, what might change after the teacher talks to you?
qa.a: Rohit might realise the joke landed much harder than intended and see that Jahnavi's love for her puppy is not babyish.

grounding: Jahnavi's fierce love and crushing upset after teasing are met with named feelings and a cool-down skill, turning intensity toward passion.

passage:
Sit, Mehak, you look like the sky is falling. Let me tell you about Alka, my friend from school, back when I was sixteen too.
One Monday Alka came skipping into class because a boy had smiled at her at the bus stop. By lunch she was shouting at our maths teacher over a mark she felt was unfair. By evening she was crying behind the water tank, sure nobody in the world understood her.
I thought she was going mad. But her grandmother, a quiet lady who sold pickles, just sat with her on the steps every evening that month. No lectures. She'd say, "Storms pass, beta. Eat something first."
Alka grew into the steadiest nurse I know. So no, you're not broken, Mehak. You are sixteen, and your Nani is right here on these steps.

qa.q: Where did Alka cry in the evening?
qa.a: She cried behind the water tank.

qa.q: How did Alka feel within that one Monday?
qa.a: She swung from giddy and excited in the morning to angry at an unfair mark at lunch to lonely and sad by evening.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Alka through that month?
qa.a: Her grandmother chose to sit with her every evening without lectures, giving her a steady adult presence while the storms passed.

qa.q: How did Alka's grandmother see Alka's storms?
qa.a: She seemed to see them as passing weather to sit through calmly, not as a problem to scold.

grounding: Nani tells Mehak about a friend whose teenage highs and lows within one day were eased by a steady adult, showing such swings are often normal.

passage:
The hostel common room at the girls' boarding school was full on visiting Sunday. Rekha had brought her younger sister Sarita's favourite snacks.
Within ten minutes Sarita had flung the packet on the floor. "You never listen! You told Mummy about my marks!" She stormed off and slammed the dormitory door so hard the warden looked up.
Rekha sat very still, face hot, feeling everyone's eyes on her. Part of her wanted to leave and not come back next month.
The warden came over. "Give her a little time. She's allowed to be angry, not to throw things."
Twenty minutes later Sarita came back, eyes red. Rekha picked up the packet. "I'm not okay with things being thrown. But I'm listening now. Tell me why the marks thing hurt." Sarita sat down beside her and, slowly, began to talk.

qa.q: What did Sarita throw on the floor?
qa.a: She flung the packet of snacks Rekha had brought on the floor.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after the door slammed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her face hot, and part of her wanted to leave and not come back next month.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Rekha, and why?
qa.a: She stayed calm, held a clear limit about throwing and waited until Sarita settled before talking, which kept them connected.

qa.q: Why might Sarita react so strongly to her marks being shared?
qa.a: She may feel exposed and betrayed that Rekha told Mummy, and her feelings come out in one big burst.

grounding: Rekha faces her teenage sister's slammed door and outburst, stays calm, holds a limit on behaviour and talks once feelings settle.
